resources.title: Cheryl David
resources.summary: Larry's wife for the show's earlier seasons, and the character whose reaction to a dispute usually settles who the audience is meant to side with.

resources.title: Jeff Greene
resources.summary: Larry's longtime friend and manager, permanently caught between Larry's schemes and his wife Susie's fury at where those schemes usually land.

resources.title: Larry David
resources.summary: The show's central figure, a fictionalised version of the real Seinfeld co-creator, who treats minor social infractions as matters of genuine principle.

resources.title: Leon Black
resources.summary: A friend of Larry's who becomes a long-term houseguest and offers a running stream of unsolicited, oddly effective advice.

resources.title: The TiVo
resources.summary: Establishes a hand gesture by which a listener may signal a storyteller to skip ahead, sparing both parties the tedium of a story's slow middle.

resources.title: The Silent Auditorium Rule
resources.summary: Establishes that narrating, questioning or reacting audibly during a film violates the shared quiet every ticket holder is presumed to have purchased.

resources.title: The Tone Violation
resources.summary: Establishes that a written message carrying an unintended harsh tone is the sender's fault, never the reader's for misreading it.

resources.title: The Anonymous Donor
resources.summary: Weighs whether an anonymous act of generosity still counts as generosity once the giver becomes desperate for someone to know it was them.

resources.title: The Stop and Chat
resources.summary: Rules on the neighbour who treats every routine sighting as an occasion for a full conversation, when a nod or a wave would fully discharge the obligation.

resources.title: The Indefinite Houseguest
resources.summary: Sets the point at which a friend's temporary stay, extended informally with no fixed end date, becomes a standing arrangement neither host nor guest ever actually agreed to.

resources.title: The Plus-One Clause
resources.summary: Governs whether a guest may bring an uninvited companion to a social function without prior clearance from the host.

resources.title: The Chat and Cut
resources.summary: Prohibits approaching someone already in a queue under the pretence of a friendly conversation, then remaining beside them as an informal, unearned cut in line.

resources.title: The Debt of Gratitude
resources.summary: Weighs how much ongoing warmth a person owes someone who has performed them a genuinely enormous, unsolicited favour, even one they never asked for.

resources.title: Sample Abuse
resources.summary: Sets the point at which repeatedly returning to a free sample counter, without any genuine intention to buy, stops being tasting and starts being an unpaid meal.

resources.title: The Footwear Mandate
resources.summary: Weighs a host's right to demand shoe removal at the door against a guest's right to be told about that rule before arriving, not on the doorstep.

resources.title: Susie Greene
resources.summary: Jeff's wife, the character the show relies on to say, at maximum volume, what everyone else is only thinking.

resources.title: The Funeral
resources.summary: Larry's golf club goes missing during a round played the same day as a funeral, and the search for it leads somewhere no one else wants him looking.

resources.title: Opening Night
resources.summary: Larry is cast in a Broadway revival of The Producers, and a season-long arc of amateur stage fright builds to a single live performance.

resources.title: The Reunion
resources.summary: Larry spends a season organising a genuine reunion special for Seinfeld, the sitcom he co-created, and finds the old cast dynamics are exactly as he left them.

resources.title: The Carpool Lane
resources.summary: Larry arranges for a companion to ride along so he can legally use the carpool lane, and must account for the arrangement when a police officer pulls him over.

resources.title: Bertram Gilfoyle
resources.summary: Pied Piper's systems architect, a self-declared LaVeyan Satanist whose deadpan contempt masks genuine infrastructure talent.

resources.title: Nelson 'Big Head' Bighetti
resources.summary: Richard Hendricks's easygoing former Hooli colleague, whose career advances repeatedly despite minimal effort or technical output.

resources.title: The Box Demo Disaster
resources.summary: The public failure of Pied Piper's enterprise compliance appliance launch, staged during Jack Barker's tenure as chief executive.

resources.title: Dinesh Chugtai
resources.summary: Pied Piper engineer and Gilfoyle's office rival, whose need for validation drives much of the pair's running feud.

resources.title: Big Head's Accidental Professorship
resources.summary: An administrative mix-up lands Big Head a paid Stanford lecturing post he keeps for years despite having no qualifications for it.

resources.title: The Middle-Out Explanation
resources.summary: The party scene where Richard is pressured into explaining Middle-Out in plain terms, producing an analogy that outlives the moment itself.

resources.title: Optimal Tip-to-Tip Efficiency
resources.summary: The season one finale, staging Nucleus's live launch collapse against Pied Piper's TechCrunch Disrupt win on the very same night.

resources.title: The Decision to Shut It Down
resources.summary: The series finale, in which Pied Piper's own team chooses to bury their most powerful breakthrough rather than release it to the world.

resources.title: Erlich Bachman
resources.summary: Bombastic early investor and incubator landlord who claims outsized credit for discovering Richard Hendricks and Pied Piper.

resources.title: Gavin Belson
resources.summary: Hooli's founder and chief executive, whose rivalry with Pied Piper runs from a rejected buyout to an IP dispute to a patent-troll lawsuit.

resources.title: Nucleus
resources.summary: Hooli's internal compression platform, rushed to market by Gavin Belson to beat Pied Piper after his acquisition offer was rejected.

resources.title: Hooli
resources.summary: Sprawling Silicon Valley technology conglomerate founded by Gavin Belson, Pied Piper's largest and most persistent rival.

resources.title: Jack Barker
resources.summary: Veteran technology executive installed as Pied Piper's CEO by the board, favouring a conventional growth-at-all-costs playbook.

resources.title: Jared Dunn
resources.summary: Pied Piper's earnest operations lead, a former Hooli senior VP who left a lucrative role to work unpaid for Richard Hendricks.

resources.title: The Compression Algorithm (Middle-Out)
resources.summary: Richard Hendricks's breakthrough lossless compression method, scoring higher on the Weissman Score than any known rival technique.

resources.title: Monica Hall
resources.summary: Raviga Capital associate and later partner who championed Pied Piper's seed investment against her own board's scepticism.

resources.title: Not Hotdog (app)
resources.summary: Jian-Yang's deliberately narrow image-recognition app, built to identify only whether a photo contains a hotdog.

resources.title: The Hooli vs Pied Piper IP and Patent Rivalry
resources.summary: Two separate legal fights Hooli brings against Pied Piper - an ownership claim over the algorithm itself, then a later patent-troll lawsuit.

resources.title: Pied Piper
resources.summary: Compression-technology startup founded by Richard Hendricks, funded by Raviga Capital and repeatedly at war with Hooli.

resources.title: PiperNet
resources.summary: Richard Hendricks's decentralised internet project, built on Middle-Out compression running across idle storage on users' own phones.

resources.title: Raviga Capital
resources.summary: Venture capital firm and Pied Piper's earliest institutional investor, holding board seats through the company's entire history.

resources.title: Richard Hendricks
resources.summary: Founder and on-again CEO of Pied Piper, the anxious engineer whose Middle-Out algorithm underpins the whole company.

resources.title: The Middle-Out Pitch at TechCrunch Disrupt
resources.summary: Pied Piper's original public unveiling of the Middle-Out compression algorithm, the moment that first drew Gavin Belson's interest.

resources.title: The Tres Commas Club
resources.summary: Investor Russ Hanneman's running fixation on the billion-dollar valuation milestone, named for the three commas in a ten-figure number.

resources.title: Borg
resources.summary: Cybernetic hive-mind species that assimilates people and technology in pursuit of perfection, and once turned Captain Picard into one of its own.

resources.title: Data
resources.summary: Self-aware android officer of the Enterprise-D whose lifelong pursuit of Human emotion led to a landmark Starfleet ruling on his own rights.

resources.title: Ferengi
resources.summary: Small, sharp-eared commerce-driven species whose entire legal and moral code is built on the Rules of Acquisition and the pursuit of profit.

resources.title: Holodeck
resources.summary: Shipboard holographic recreation facility on later Starfleet vessels, whose safety protocols have famously failed in some of Starfleet's strangest recorded incidents.

resources.title: James T. Kirk
resources.summary: Iconic Starfleet captain who led the USS Enterprise on its historic five-year mission and became the only cadet to beat a legendarily unwinnable test.

resources.title: Jean-Luc Picard
resources.summary: Measured, diplomatic Enterprise-D captain famed for his command of Shakespeare, his archaeology hobby and his survival of assimilation by the Borg.

resources.title: Klingon
resources.summary: Warrior species from the homeworld Qo'noS whose Empire moved from bitter Federation rival to uneasy ally across generations of shared history.

resources.title: Leonard McCoy
resources.summary: Blunt, deeply humane chief medical officer of the USS Enterprise, whose scepticism of the transporter never once stopped him from doing his job.

resources.title: The Best of Both Worlds
resources.summary: The Borg abduct and assimilate Captain Picard as Locutus, forcing First Officer Riker to lead the Enterprise-D against the fleet's most devastating defeat.

resources.title: Caretaker
resources.summary: A search for missing Maquis rebels flings USS Voyager seventy thousand light years into the Delta Quadrant, starting the crew's long journey home.

resources.title: The City on the Edge of Forever
resources.summary: Kirk and Spock pursue a delirious McCoy through a time portal to 1930s Earth, where saving the woman Kirk loves would unravel history itself.

resources.title: In the Pale Moonlight
resources.summary: Captain Sisko compromises his own principles to draw the Romulan Star Empire into the Dominion War, then has to live with how he did it.

resources.title: Nyota Uhura
resources.summary: Enterprise communications officer and gifted linguist whose skill broke first-contact deadlocks, in a role that made real television history too.

resources.title: Phaser
resources.summary: Starfleet's standard energy sidearm, built around a strict stun-first doctrine that runs from non-lethal incapacitation up to full disintegration.

resources.title: Romulan
resources.summary: Secretive militarised species descended from Vulcans who rejected logic, ruling the Romulan Star Empire from behind a veil of cloaked ships.

resources.title: Spock
resources.summary: Half-Vulcan, half-Human science officer of the USS Enterprise, famed for cool logic, the Vulcan mind meld and a lifelong friendship with Kirk and McCoy.

resources.title: Transporter
resources.summary: Starfleet's matter-energy transport system, standard on every vessel, with a track record strong enough to survive its own most famous malfunction.

resources.title: Tricorder
resources.summary: Handheld Starfleet scanning device carried on every away mission, with medical and science variants tailored to the officer using it.

resources.title: USS Defiant
resources.summary: Compact, heavily armed Starfleet warship built after the Borg's attack on the fleet, later a mainstay of Deep Space Nine during the Dominion War.

resources.title: USS Enterprise
resources.summary: Storied line of Starfleet flagships, from Kirk's original five-year mission to Picard's Enterprise-D, each a byword for Starfleet exploration itself.

resources.title: USS Voyager
resources.summary: Intrepid-class Starfleet vessel, commanded by Kathryn Janeway, stranded in the Delta Quadrant and forced to spend seventy-five years finding a way home.

resources.title: Vulcan
resources.summary: Logic-driven humanoid species from the planet Vulcan, whose culture was rebuilt around emotional control after Surak's teachings ended ancient wars.

resources.title: Warp Drive
resources.summary: Starfleet's faster-than-light propulsion system, powered by a dilithium-regulated matter-antimatter reaction, and the technology that first brought Vulcans to Earth.

resources.title: Worf
resources.summary: Klingon Starfleet officer raised by Human parents after a Romulan attack, valued for his combat skill and unbending code of honour.
